description: How US dollars and divided Berlin made the Cold War a concrete European reality.
content_html:
America Steps In: the Truman Doctrine 1947

By early 1947, Britain told the United States it could no longer afford to support the Greek government, which was fighting a communist insurgency. President Harry S. Truman responded on 12 March 1947 with a speech to Congress that became known as the Truman Doctrine. He asked Congress for $400 million to aid Greece and Turkey, framing it as a choice between freedom and totalitarianism. This speech marked the formal beginning of containment as official US policy.

The Truman Doctrine was a significant break from America's traditional reluctance to commit to peacetime alliances. Some historians see it as a genuine defensive response to Soviet pressure in Eastern Europe; others, such as the revisionist historian William Appleman Williams, argue it reflected US economic interests and an aggressive projection of American power. Both readings help explain how the Cold War became a global confrontation rather than a purely European one.

Key Fact

On 12 March 1947 Truman asked Congress for $400 million to aid Greece and Turkey, declaring that the USA would support free peoples resisting communist takeover. This speech launched the policy of containment.

Rebuilding Europe: the Marshall Plan 1947

US Secretary of State George C. Marshall announced his European Recovery Programme on 5 June 1947 at Harvard University. Between 1948 and 1952 the USA provided approximately $13 billion in economic aid to sixteen Western European nations. The aim was to rebuild war-shattered economies, create stable markets for American goods, and remove the conditions — poverty and unemployment — in which communism might flourish.

The Soviet Union refused the offer and, through Cominform, pressured Poland and Czechoslovakia to reject it too. Stalin publicly branded Marshall Aid “dollar imperialism”, seeing it as a mechanism to extend US economic influence. From a Western perspective it was a generous reconstruction package; from the Soviet perspective it was a tool of ideological competition. Historians present both as legitimate readings of the same policy.

After 1945 Germany was divided into four occupation zones controlled by the USA, USSR, Britain and France. The Western powers merged their zones economically — the American and British zones became Bizonia in January 1947, with France joining later. When the Western powers introduced a new currency, the Deutschmark, in June 1948, Stalin saw it as a step towards a permanent Western German state hostile to the USSR.

The result was two separate German states. The Federal Republic of Germany (FRG) was established in May 1949; the German Democratic Republic (GDR) followed in October 1949. Germany’s division lasted four decades and became one of the defining symbols of the Cold War.

The Berlin Blockade and Airlift 1948–1949

Berlin lay inside the Soviet zone but was also divided into four sectors. On 24 June 1948, Stalin ordered all road, rail and canal routes from West Germany to West Berlin to be closed, cutting off two million people from food, fuel and other supplies. This was the Berlin Blockade. Stalin gambled that the West would rather abandon Berlin than risk war.

The Western response was the Berlin Airlift, organised by US General Lucius D. Clay and British Foreign Secretary Ernest Bevin. At its peak, Allied aircraft landed in West Berlin every 45 seconds, delivering coal, food and medicine. After 323 days Stalin lifted the blockade on 12 May 1949 — a humiliating climbdown that demonstrated Western resolve without triggering open conflict.

Key Fact

The Berlin Blockade lasted 323 days (24 June 1948 – 12 May 1949). The successful airlift showed the Western powers would defend Berlin without direct military confrontation, boosting Western credibility and hastening the formation of NATO in April 1949.

The Berlin crisis accelerated talks about collective Western defence. On 4 April 1949, twelve nations — including the USA, Britain, France, Canada and others — signed the North Atlantic Treaty, creating NATO. Article 5 committed every member to treat an armed attack on one as an attack on all. This was the first peacetime military alliance the United States had ever joined, marking a decisive break from isolationism.

The Soviet Union responded in September 1947 by establishing Cominform to coordinate communist parties across Eastern Europe. After NATO’s founding, the USSR began to build its own defensive architecture, culminating in the Warsaw Pact of 1955. The formation of rival military blocs hardened the division of Europe into two competing spheres.
exam_tip_html: When asked to “outline” events of this period, make sure your answer has two distinct, developed points — not a list of bullet facts. For example, if asked to outline the Berlin Blockade, describe what Stalin did, then explain why the Western response mattered. Time-frame discipline is essential: the Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan are 1947–1952 material, not 1945 or 1953 — always anchor your facts to the correct year range or you risk losing marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Truman Doctrine (March 1947) committed the USA to containing communism, framing the Cold War as an ideological struggle between freedom and totalitarianism.
  • Marshall Aid ($13 billion, 1948–1952) rebuilt Western Europe and removed the poverty that could fuel communist movements; Stalin rejected it and branded it dollar imperialism.
  • The Berlin Blockade (1948–1949) and the airlift that defeated it demonstrated Western resolve, while Germany’s division into the FRG and GDR (both 1949) made the Iron Curtain a physical reality.

practice_questions.text: Outline two consequences of the Truman Doctrine for Cold War relations in Europe.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two distinct developed consequences, each with a specific supporting detail (e.g. containment policy formalised; Western bloc consolidation accelerated). Secure: Two identified consequences with some development. Developing: Two consequences identified but not developed beyond a basic statement. Emerging: One brief point.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the USSR rejected the Marshall Plan.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons, each with specific factual support and a clear link to the question (e.g. Stalin feared economic dependency on the USA; Cominform used to enforce rejection on Eastern bloc states). Secure: Two reasons developed with some supporting detail. Developing: Two reasons identified but development is limited or repetitive. Emerging: One basic reason.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Berlin Airlift was a significant turning point in the early Cold War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument for significance with specific evidence (323-day duration; 45-second landing intervals; Soviet climbdown) linked clearly to changed Cold War dynamics. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail but less developed analysis. Developing: Some explanation with limited detail. Emerging: Brief descriptive points.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Berlin Blockade 1948–1949.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two clear features, each supported by specific accurate detail (e.g. Stalin closed road, rail and canal routes; the blockade lasted 323 days). Secure: Two features with some supporting detail. Developing: Two features identified but without supporting detail. Emerging: One brief feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the USA introduced the Marshall Plan in 1947.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more well-developed causes linked to the Marshall Plan's purpose, with specific supporting detail and causal analysis (economic: preventing communist expansion in war-weakened states; political: undercutting Soviet influence). Secure: Two causes developed with relevant detail. Developing: One cause developed or two causes with limited development. Emerging: Simple statement of cause.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Germany was divided into two states by 1949.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained explanation identifying multiple causal factors (post-war Allied disagreement, introduction of Deutschmark, Berlin Blockade) linked coherently. Specific detail required. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence. Developing: Some explanation but development limited. Emerging: Brief descriptive account.

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Truman Doctrine announced?
How much aid did the Marshall Plan provide between 1948 and 1952?
flashcard_questions.a: Approximately $13 billion to sixteen Western European nations.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did Stalin reject Marshall Aid?
flashcard_questions.a: He saw it as 'dollar imperialism' — a tool to extend US economic and ideological influence in Europe.
The merged American and British occupation zones of Germany created in January 1947.

flashcard_questions.q: When did the Berlin Blockade begin and end?
How did the West respond to the Berlin Blockade?
flashcard_questions.a: With the Berlin Airlift, flying supplies into West Berlin; at peak, aircraft landed every 45 seconds.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the outcome of the Berlin Blockade for Stalin?
flashcard_questions.a: A humiliating climbdown — he lifted the blockade without achieving his aim of forcing the West from Berlin.

What did Article 5 of the NATO Treaty commit members to?
flashcard_questions.a: Treating an armed attack on one member as an attack on all.

flashcard_questions.q: George C. Marshall — what role did he hold and what did he announce?
flashcard_questions.a: US Secretary of State; announced the European Recovery Programme on 5 June 1947.
Soviet-led Communist Information Bureau founded September 1947 to coordinate Eastern bloc communist parties.

glossary_terms.definition: 33rd US President (1945–1953) who declared US commitment to resisting communist expansion worldwide.
President Truman's 1947 declaration that the USA would support free peoples resisting subjugation by armed minorities or outside pressures.
US foreign policy strategy aimed at preventing the further spread of Soviet communism, first articulated in 1947.
US Secretary of State who announced the European Recovery Programme in June 1947, offering American aid to rebuild war-devastated European economies.
The Communist Information Bureau, founded in September 1947 to coordinate Soviet-aligned communist parties across Europe.
The merged American and British occupation zones of Germany created in 1947 as the foundation for a future West German state.
The West German state established in May 1949 from the three Western occupation zones, aligned with NATO.
The East German state established in October 1949 under Soviet influence.
Stalin's 1948–1949 attempt to force the Western powers out of West Berlin by cutting all land supply routes into the city.
The Western airlift from June 1948 to May 1949 that supplied West Berlin by aircraft after Soviet forces blocked all land routes.
The North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, founded in April 1949 as a collective defence alliance committing members to treat an attack on one as an attack on all.
